transcript: Welcome to Course 3: Plagiarism, Turnitin & Research Integrity. In this opening lecture, we demystify what plagiarism actually means in contemporary higher education.

Most students believe plagiarism is only word-for-word copy-pasting without quotation marks. However, Turnitin and university ethics committees define plagiarism along a broad spectrum: from verbatim copying, to 'patchwriting' where sentence structure is preserved while substituting synonyms, to structural and conceptual appropriation without citation.

Under the Higher Education Commission (HEC) of Pakistan, submitting someone else's work, paying third-party commercial essay mills to write your dissertation, or recycling your own previously graded coursework without authorization can result in blacklisting, degree revocation, and disciplinary expulsion.

True academic integrity is not merely about beating an algorithm or keeping your similarity below 19%. It is about honest scholarship: transparently attributing every fact, definition, and idea that did not originate in your own mind.
key: Plagiarism is an ethical breach covering verbatim copying, patchwriting, idea theft, and unauthorized self-recycling.
Turnitin does not detect 'plagiarism'—it calculates text similarity against millions of web pages, student papers, and subscription journals.
Patchwriting (swapping synonyms while retaining another author's exact clause structure) is classified as plagiarism even if a citation is present.
The HEC policy enforces penalties ranging from thesis revision and grade failure to public blacklisting and degree cancellation.
